(''non'' Ker Gawl.: [[Ipomoea tuberculata|preoccupied]]) }} '''''Ipomoea cairica''''' is a [[vine|vining]], [[herbaceous]], [[perennial]] plant with palmate leaves and large, showy white to lavender flowers. A species of [[Ipomoea|morning glory]], it has many common names, including '''mile-a-minute vine''', '''Messina creeper''', '''Cairo morning glory''', '''coast morning glory''' and '''railroad creeper'''.[https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=IPCA Ipomoea cairica (L.) Sweet], USDA PLANTSColmeiro, Miguel: "Dictionary of the diverse vulgar names of many usual or notable plants of the old and new world", Madrid, 1871. The species name ''cairica'' translates to "from [[Cairo]]", the city where this species was first collected.[http://pza.sanbi.org/ipomoea-cairica-var-cairica Ipomoea cairica (L.) Sweet var. cairica] SA National Biodiversity Institute ==Description== A hairless, slim climber with [[bulb]]ous roots and lignescented base, its leaves are stalked with 2 to 6 cm long [[petiole (botany)|petiole]]s. The leaf blade is ovate to circular in outline, 3 to 10 cm long and 6 to 9 cm wide. It is divided into five to seven segments, these are [[lanceolate]], ovate or elliptic, entire and pointed at the tip and base. Often pseudo side-leaves are formed.Carranza, E. (2008). «Diversity of the Genus Ipomoea L. (CONVOLVULACEAE) in the State of Michoacán, Mexico». Flora of the Bajío and Adjacent Regions . Complementary Fascicle XXIII. The [[Lavender (color)|lavender]]-coloured [[inflorescence]]s are one to a [[cymes|cyme]]. The flower [[Peduncle (botany)|stalks]] are 12 to 20 mm long, the [[sepal]]s are 6 to 8 mm long, ovate and sting-pointed. The [[Crown (botany)|crown]] is funnel-shaped, 4 to 6 cm long and violet colored. The [[stamen]]s and the [[Style (botany)|stylus]] do not protrude beyond the crown. The [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] is hairless. The fruits are spherical capsules approximately 1 cm in diameter containing one or two hairy seeds. Each fruit matures at about 1 cm across and contains hairy seeds.S. Dressler, M. Schmidt, G. Zizka (ed.): African plants - A Photo Guide. Senckenberg, Frankfurt / Main 2014. The vine [[Free-flowering|blooms occasionally]] throughout the months, but more profusely from spring to summer.[https://www.bushlandperth.org.au/weeds/coast-morning-glory-or-mile-a-minute/ COAST MORNING GLORY OR MILE-A-MINUTE] Urban Bushland Council WA IncCarranza, E. (2007). «Family Convolvulaceae». Flora of the Bajío and Adjacent Regions . Fascicle 151 ==Range== Its exact native range is uncertain, though it is believed to originate from a rather wide area, ranging from [[Cape Verde]] to the [[Arabian Peninsula]], including northern [[Africa]], [[tropical Africa]] and the [[Mediterranean]]. It covers walls, fences or trees, with stems that can measure more than {{convert|10|m}} in length. The altitude at which it has been recorded ranges from {{convert|250|m}} to {{convert|2250|m|abbr=on}}.Invasive species group, Plants invasive for the natural environments of New Caledonia, Nouméa, Agency for the prevention and compensation of agricultural or natural calamities (APICAN), January 2012, 222 p., pp. 110-111 ==Invasive species== Because of [[Hemerochory|human dispersal]], it occurs today on most continents as an [[introduced species]] and is sometimes a [[noxious weed]] and an [[invasive species]], such as along the coast of [[New South Wales]]. As well as in the United States, where it occurs in Hawaii, California, all the gulf coast states, as well as Arkansas and Missouri. It also occurs in [[Brazil]], where it is used in [[traditional medicine]].{{Cite journal|last1=Tognon|first1=G. B.|last2=Petry|first2=C.|date=2012|title=Estaquia de Ipomoea cairica (L.) Sweet|journal=Revista Brasileira de Plantas Medicinais|language=pt|volume=14|issue=3 |pages=470–475|doi=10.1590/S1516-05722012000300008|issn=1516-0572|doi-access=free}} It is a widespread [[garden escape]] in southeast Australia.[https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Ipomoea~cairica Ipomoea cairica (L.) Sweet] PlantNET (The NSW Plant Information Network System). Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust, Sydney. Retrieved 30 December 2023. ==Cultivation== Some plant nurseries sell this plant as an [[ornamental plant]] thanks to its showy purple flowers and as well for its fast growth to quickly cover unsightly fences or walls. It can grow as a separate plant if [[cuttings (plant)|snapped]] during attempted removal process.[http://www.georgiavines.com/cart/index.php?main_page=product_info&products_id=550] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201029194544/http://www.georgiavines.com/cart/index.php?main_page=product_info&products_id=550 |date=2020-10-29 }}, Georgia Vines Cart The plant causes respiratory symptoms if ingested. Ipomoea cairica 'alba', also known as 'white Cairo morning glory', is a [[variety (botany)|variety]] with white flowers.[https://www.buyrareseeds.com/fresh-seeds/index.php?main_page=product_info&products_id=921 Ipomoea cairica Alba| Palmate Morning Glory] Buy Rare Seeds. Retrieved 30 December 2023. == Uses == Most parts of the plant are edible. Its roots are reportedly edible when cooked{{Cite web |date=2010-11-07 |title=Ipomoea cairica - Mile A Minute Vine, Koali Ai, Koali, Kowali |url=https://wildlifeofhawaii.com/flowers/1607/ipomoea-cairica-mile-a-minute-vine/ |access-date=2025-07-09 |website=Hawaiian Plants and Tropical Flowers |language=en-US}} and its leaves are eaten when young. [[Zulu people]] use the plant medicinally, where they make a concoction with its crushed leaves and drink it to heal [[rash]]es and fever.
